Cell Structure.intro: All living things are made of cells. Understanding the differences between cell types is fundamental to GCSE Biology. There are two main types of cells: prokaryotic (like bacteria) and eukaryotic (like plant and animal cells).

sections.title: Animal Cells
sections.text: Animal cells are eukaryotic cells containing a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
points: Nucleus — contains DNA, controls cell activity
Cell membrane — controls what enters and leaves the cell
Cytoplasm — jelly-like fluid where chemical reactions occur
Mitochondria — site of aerobic respiration, produces ATP
Ribosomes — site of protein synthesis

sections.title: Plant Cells
sections.text: Plant cells are also eukaryotic but have additional structures not found in animal cells.
points: All animal cell structures PLUS:
Cell wall — made of cellulose, provides strength and support
Chloroplasts — contain chlorophyll, site of photosynthesis
Permanent vacuole — filled with cell sap, maintains turgor pressure

sections.title: Prokaryotic Cells (Bacteria)
sections.text: Prokaryotic cells are smaller and simpler than eukaryotic cells — they have no nucleus.
points: No nucleus — DNA floats freely in cytoplasm as a single loop
Plasmids — small extra loops of DNA
Cell wall — made of different material to plant cell walls
Flagellum — tail used for movement (some bacteria)
No membrane-bound organelles

callout.label: Key Comparison
callout.text: Prokaryotic cells are typically 1–10 μm. Eukaryotic cells are typically 10–100 μm. Prokaryotic = no true nucleus. Eukaryotic = has nucleus.

keyTerms.def: Cells with a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane
Cells without a true nucleus — DNA is free in the cytoplasm
A specialised structure within a cell that carries out a specific function
The jelly-like substance filling the cell where reactions take place
Organelles where aerobic respiration occurs to release energy
Tiny organelles where proteins are made (protein synthesis)

examTips: Always list plant cell structures as animal structures PLUS the three extras (cell wall, chloroplasts, vacuole).
Bacteria are prokaryotic — they have ribosomes but NO mitochondria or chloroplasts.
The cell membrane is present in ALL cell types — don't confuse it with the cell wall.
commonMistakes: Saying cells walls are made of chitin — that's fungi. Plant cell walls are made of cellulose.
Forgetting that both plant and animal cells have mitochondria — only plant cells have chloroplasts.
Confusing the cell membrane (all cells) with the cell wall (plants and bacteria only).
Cell Structure.mnemonic: MCRN — every cell has a Membrane, Cytoplasm, Ribosomes and Nucleus. Plants add 3 extras: Cell Wall, Chloroplasts, Vacuole (WCV — 'We Can Vacuolate').
Cell Structure.diagram: Differences between simple animal and plant cells, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0) — View on Wikimedia Commons
clozePassages: The nucleus is found in both animal and plant cells and contains DNA, which controls cell activity. The cell membrane surrounds every cell and controls the movement of substances in and out. The cytoplasm is a jelly-like fluid where chemical reactions take place. Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, releasing energy for the cell. Ribosomes are tiny structures where protein synthesis occurs.

Plant cells have several structures not found in animal cells. The cell wall is made of cellulose and provides strength and support. Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis. The vacuole is a large, fluid-filled space that helps maintain the shape of the cell. Animal cells do not have a cell wall, chloroplasts, or a permanent vacuole.

Prokaryotic cells are much smaller and simpler than eukaryotic cells. Prokaryotic cells, such as bacteria, have no true nucleus — their DNA floats freely in the cytoplasm. They also lack membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotic cells, including animal and plant cells, have a nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane. The size of a prokaryotic cell is typically 1-10 micrometres.

Cells can be observed using a light microscope or an electron microscope. The light microscope uses visible light and can magnify up to around 2000 times. The electron microscope uses a beam of electrons and has much greater magnification and resolution, allowing sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes to be seen clearly.

Microscopy.intro: Microscopes allow us to see cells and structures too small for the naked eye. Understanding how microscopes work and how to calculate magnification is essential for GCSE Biology.

sections.title: Types of Microscope
points: Light microscope — uses light and lenses; magnification up to ×2000; resolution ~200nm; can view living specimens
Electron microscope — uses electrons; magnification up to ×2,000,000; resolution ~0.2nm; can see sub-cellular structures; specimens must be dead

sections.title: Magnification Formula
sections.text: You must be able to use the magnification formula in the exam:

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Magnification = Image size ÷ Actual size  |  Rearranged: Actual size = Image size ÷ Magnification

points: Always use the same units for image size and actual size
Convert between mm and μm: 1 mm = 1000 μm
If asked for magnification, divide image by actual
If asked for actual size, divide image by magnification

sections.title: Units of Measurement
points: 1 metre (m) = 1000 millimetres (mm)
1 mm = 1000 micrometres (μm)
1 μm = 1000 nanometres (nm)
Most cells are measured in μm; viruses and molecules in nm

keyTerms.def: How many times larger an image appears compared to the actual object
The ability to distinguish between two points — how much detail you can see
Unit of measurement equal to one thousandth of a millimetre
Unit of measurement equal to one millionth of a millimetre
Microscope using a beam of electrons — much higher magnification and resolution than light microscopes

examTips: Show your working clearly in magnification calculations — you can get method marks even with a wrong final answer.
Remember: electron microscopes have higher magnification AND higher resolution than light microscopes.
Check units carefully — the question may give image size in mm but actual size in μm. Convert first!
Microscopy.mnemonic: Formula triangle: cover what you want to find. Cover I (image) = M × A. Cover M (magnification) = I ÷ A. Cover A (actual) = I ÷ M. Say: 'I aM Actual' — Image = Magnification × Actual.
Microscopy.diagram: Compound microscope diagram, Wikimedia Commons (Public Domain) — View on Wikimedia Commons
commonMistakes: Confusing magnification with resolution — they are different things.
Forgetting to convert units before calculating — always use the same units.
Saying electron microscopes can view living cells — they cannot, specimens must be dead.
clozePassages: A light microscope passes light through a sample to produce a magnified image. The total magnification is calculated by multiplying the eyepiece lens by the objective lens. Resolution is the ability to distinguish between two points — a higher resolution gives a clearer image. Light microscopes have a resolution of about 200 nanometres, which limits what can be seen.

The electron microscope uses a beam of electrons instead of light, giving a much higher resolution than a light microscope. This allows scientists to see sub-cellular structures such as mitochondria and ribosomes in detail. Electron microscopes can magnify up to 2 million times. However, they are expensive and samples must be prepared in a vacuum.

When preparing a slide for microscopy, a thin sample is placed on a microscope slide and covered with a coverslip. A stain such as iodine or methylene blue is often used to make structures more visible. The image produced is called a magnified image. The actual size of a specimen can be calculated using the formula: size = image size ÷ magnification.

Cell Division.intro: Cells divide to allow organisms to grow, repair damaged tissue, and reproduce. The main type of cell division you need to know for Combined Science is mitosis.

sections.title: The Cell Cycle
sections.text: Before a cell can divide, it must grow and copy its DNA. The cell cycle has two main phases:
points: Interphase — cell grows, DNA is replicated, organelles are copied
Mitosis — nucleus divides, then cytoplasm divides (cytokinesis)

sections.title: Mitosis
sections.text: Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells. It is used for: growth, repair of damaged tissues, and asexual reproduction.
points: Chromosomes are copied so each new cell gets a full set
Produces 2 daughter cells
Daughter cells are genetically IDENTICAL to the parent cell
Each daughter cell is diploid (has the full number of chromosomes)

callout.label: Memory Aid
callout.text: Mitosis = Makes Identical Twins. Both daughter cells have the same DNA as the parent.

sections.title: Cancer
sections.text: Cancer occurs when the cell cycle goes out of control — cells divide uncontrollably to form a tumour.
points: Caused by mutations in the DNA that control cell division
Can be triggered by radiation, chemicals (carcinogens) or viruses
Benign tumour — does not spread; malignant tumour — invades other tissues (cancer)

keyTerms.def: Cell division that produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells
Thread-like structure made of DNA carrying genetic information
The period between cell divisions when DNA is replicated and the cell grows
A cell containing two complete sets of chromosomes (in humans, 46)
A mass of abnormal cells formed by uncontrolled cell division

examTips: Mitosis produces 2 identical cells. Always state 'genetically identical' in exam answers.
You do not need to know the individual stages (prophase, metaphase etc.) for Combined Science.
Cancer = uncontrolled mitosis. Benign tumours don't spread; malignant ones do.
Cell Division.mnemonic: MIT-osis = Makes Identical Twins. Interphase = 'I prepare' (grow + copy DNA). Result: 2 cells, same DNA, diploid.
Cell Division.diagram: Animal cell cycle diagram, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0) — View on Wikimedia Commons
commonMistakes: Saying mitosis produces gametes — gametes are produced by meiosis (not on Combined Science spec).
Forgetting that DNA replication happens BEFORE mitosis, during interphase.
Confusing chromosomes with genes — chromosomes contain many genes.
clozePassages: Mitosis is a type of cell division that produces two daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell. Before mitosis begins, the DNA is copied so that each daughter cell receives a full set of chromosomes. Mitosis is used for growth, repair, and asexual reproduction. Human body cells contain 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs.

The cell cycle consists of a period of growth and DNA replication followed by cell division. During the growth phase, the cell increases in size and copies its DNA. The chromosomes then condense and the cell divides by mitosis to produce two identical daughter cells. The cell cycle is tightly controlled — loss of control can lead to cancer.

Meiosis is a type of cell division that produces four genetically different daughter cells, each with half the number of chromosomes of the parent cell. It occurs in the reproductive organs and produces gametes — sperm and egg cells. Each gamete contains 23 chromosomes. When two gametes fuse at fertilisation, the full 46 chromosomes are restored.

Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide and develop into many different cell types. Embryonic stem cells can become any type of cell in the body. Adult stem cells are more limited and can only form certain cell types. Stem cells have potential uses in medicine, such as treating diabetes and paralysis, though their use raises ethical issues.

Transport.intro: Substances move in and out of cells by three processes: diffusion, osmosis, and active transport. Understanding the differences between these is essential.

sections.title: Diffusion
sections.text: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from an area of high concentration to low concentration (down a concentration gradient). It is passive — no energy needed.
points: Gases and small molecules move by diffusion (e.g. O₂, CO₂, glucose)
Rate increases with: steeper gradient, higher temperature, larger surface area, shorter distance
Examples: gas exchange in lungs, CO₂ leaving cells

sections.title: Osmosis
sections.text: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules from a dilute solution (high water potential) to a concentrated solution (low water potential) through a partially permeable membrane.
points: Only water moves by osmosis (not solutes)
Requires a partially permeable membrane
If a cell is in dilute solution — water enters — cell swells (turgid)
If a cell is in concentrated solution — water leaves — cell shrinks (plasmolysis in plants, crenation in animals)

callout.label: Exam Definition
callout.text: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.

sections.title: Active Transport
sections.text: Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient (from low to high concentration). It requires energy from respiration.
points: Goes AGAINST the concentration gradient
Requires ATP (energy from respiration)
Uses carrier proteins
Example: uptake of mineral ions by plant roots; glucose absorption in the gut

keyTerms.def: Net movement of particles from high to low concentration — passive, no energy needed
Movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from high to low water potential
Movement of substances against the concentration gradient using energy from respiration
The difference in concentration between two areas
A membrane that allows some molecules through but not others
A plant cell that has absorbed water by osmosis and is firm/swollen

examTips: The full definition of osmosis must mention: water molecules, partially permeable membrane, water potential (or concentration gradient).
Active transport always needs energy — if the question says no energy is used, it cannot be active transport.
In osmosis questions, 'dilute' = high water potential and 'concentrated' = low water potential.
commonMistakes: Saying osmosis is the movement of water from low to high concentration — it is from high water potential (dilute) to low water potential (concentrated).
Forgetting that active transport needs energy but diffusion and osmosis do not.
Applying osmosis to gases — osmosis is water only.
Transport.mnemonic: DOA — Diffusion (no energy, down gradient), Osmosis (water only, through membrane), Active transport (Against gradient, needs ATP). Or: 'Dead Or Alive' — Diffusion & Osmosis are passive (no energy needed), Active transport needs energy.
Transport.diagram: Osmosis diagram, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0) — View on Wikimedia Commons
clozePassages: Diffusion is the movement of particles from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration. It is a passive process requiring no energy. The rate of diffusion is affected by the concentration gradient, temperature, and surface area. Oxygen and carbon dioxide move in and out of cells by diffusion across the cell membrane.

Osmosis is the movement of water molecules from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane. It is a special type of diffusion involving only water. If a cell is placed in a solution more dilute than its contents, water enters by osmosis and the cell swells. If placed in a more concentrated solution, water leaves and the cell shrinks.

Active transport moves substances from a low concentration to a high concentration — against the concentration gradient. It requires energy from respiration and involves carrier proteins in the cell membrane. Active transport is used in the gut to absorb glucose and mineral ions into the blood even when their concentration in the blood is already high.

Specialised Cells.intro: Most cells in multicellular organisms become specialised to carry out specific functions. Their structure is adapted to their job — this is called cell specialisation.

sections.title: Sperm Cell
points: Function: fertilise an egg cell
Long tail (flagellum) for swimming
Many mitochondria to provide energy for swimming
Acrosome (enzyme-filled tip) to penetrate the egg
Streamlined head shape
Haploid — contains half the normal number of chromosomes

sections.title: Egg Cell (Ovum)
points: Function: to be fertilised and develop into an embryo
Large cell with lots of cytoplasm containing nutrients for the developing embryo
Haploid nucleus
After fertilisation, the zona pellucida (outer layer) changes to prevent more sperm entering

sections.title: Ciliated Epithelial Cell
points: Function: move mucus and trapped particles up and away from the lungs
Covered in tiny hair-like cilia that beat rhythmically
Found lining the trachea and bronchi
Many mitochondria to power the movement of cilia

sections.title: Root Hair Cell
points: Function: absorb water and mineral ions from soil
Long hair-like extension increases surface area
No chloroplasts (underground — no light)
Many mitochondria for active transport of mineral ions

sections.title: Nerve Cell (Neurone)
points: Function: transmit electrical impulses
Very long — can reach from spinal cord to toe
Branched endings (dendrites) to receive signals from many cells
Myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds up impulse transmission

keyTerms.def: A cell adapted in structure to carry out a specific function
The process by which a cell becomes specialised for a particular function
A whip-like tail used for cell movement (e.g. in sperm cells)
Tiny hair-like projections on cell surfaces used to move substances
A cell with only one set of chromosomes (half the normal number)

examTips: Always link the structural feature to the function — e.g. 'many mitochondria to provide energy for active transport/movement'.
Root hair cells have no chloroplasts — they are underground and cannot photosynthesize.
Sperm and egg cells are haploid so that when they fuse the resulting cell (zygote) is diploid.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to explain WHY a feature is an adaptation — not just what it is.
Saying root hair cells have chloroplasts — they don't, as they are underground.
Confusing cilia (move mucus) with flagellum (used for swimming by sperm).
Specialised Cells.mnemonic: SCENE — Sperm (tail+mitochondria), Ciliated (cilia+mitochondria), Egg (nutrients+large), Nerve (long+dendrites), root hair Extension (surface area). Each cell: think WHAT it does → WHY its shape helps.

clozePassages: Cells become specialised through a process called differentiation, where they develop specific structures to carry out particular functions. A sperm cell has a streamlined shape, a tail for movement, and many mitochondria to provide energy. An egg cell contains nutrients to support the developing embryo and has a membrane that changes after fertilisation to prevent more sperm entering.

Red blood cells are adapted to carry oxygen efficiently. They have a biconcave shape which increases surface area for gas exchange. They contain large amounts of haemoglobin, which binds to oxygen. Red blood cells have no nucleus, giving more space for haemoglobin. White blood cells are part of the immune system and can change shape to engulf pathogens.

Nerve cells (neurones) are long and thin to carry electrical impulses over long distances. They have many dendrites to receive signals from other neurones. The axon is covered by a myelin sheath which speeds up the transmission of impulses. Muscle cells contain protein fibres that can contract and relax, and they have many mitochondria to provide energy for movement.

Root hair cells have a large surface area due to their long, hair-like extension, which increases the rate of water absorption by osmosis. They also absorb mineral ions by active transport. Xylem cells are hollow and have thickened walls strengthened with lignin, allowing them to transport water up the plant and provide support.
